metadata.title: I Was Fixing a Fuel Tank - It Did Not Go Well
metadata.description:
The 1996 Chevy K3500 is back and it's pushing me to the edge...

Featuring music by Karl Casey @ White Bat Audio

captions.text: This is the auxiliary fuel tank from a '96 Chevy K3500. The sending unit is rotten. The tabs that hold the sending unit are rotten. The whole top of the tank has collapsed. And probably the biggest problem, the surface for the O-ring that seals the sending unit is no longer round or flat. It's not even close. There's no way that it would ever seal. These tanks are are pretty rare. They only use them in cab and chassis trucks. You can't get a new one. Anything used, at least in our area, is going to be as bad or worse. So, I want to fix it. I just haven't quite figured out how we're going to do it. I think the plastic fuel tank is a great idea, but GM still found a way to screw it up. They molded these metal lock tabs right into the plastic. And when the top of the tank sags, the notch for the fuel pump becomes a salt water soaking pool that rots out anything metal. If the locking tabs just rotted off, that really wouldn't be the end of the world. The problem is they rot inside the plastic. That causes rust jacking that deforms the hole for the pump into a kind of a lumpy pentagon. I've seen them so swollen you can't even get the pump out without cutting away the plastic. Kind of hurts to say this, but Chrysler did something right. Not this. This is all wrong. But this is pretty good. Same plastic tank, same metal lock tabs, same metal lock ring, but no salt water soaking pool. So, no problems. This is a 12-year-old truck. I just took the fuel pump out, put a new one in. No problem. Yeah. >> Really? Come on. I can pull the top of the tank up, but it won't stay that way on its own. It needs some kind of a brace. I can't think of a good way to do that from the outside, so I'm going to make a jack to prop it up from the inside. >> [music] [music] >> The O-ring groove is just too far gone. It's never going to seal. I thought about making some kind of jig to try and recut it, but power tools and fuel vapors usually don't go well together. It's definitely an interesting aroma in the shop this morning. It's a combination of rotten gasoline, spray paint, burning rubber, and burning steel. It's not altogether unpleasant. The tank is clean. I've got the top sort of chiseled and sanded flat and smooth or as good as it can get. The brace on the inside will keep the tank from collapsing. I'm just going to leave it in there. I don't I don't think it'll hurt anything. This rubber gasket's going to take the place of the original O-ring and this steel ring is going to take the place of the original lock ring. Just to be safe, I'm going to use a little bit of this Seal-All. Okay. Looks like zero to me. That'll work. I put an extra bead of that Seal-All around the outside of the gasket. I just thought it might help keep water from creeping underneath. I don't It probably doesn't need it. Anyway, it looks pretty good. Let's put this baby back together. >> [bell] >> Well, that might be a problem. It was frozen the last time I lifted it. I guess we'll see how much spills out. >> [bell] >> All right. Well, not so bad. You may have noticed the thing I put in the tank isn't really a pump. It's just a sending unit. This is the actual pump and it's also junk. Luckily, it's super easy to replace. Actually, this whole job is pretty easy. I wish every truck had a tilting bed. The auxiliary fuel tank is controlled by this balance control module. When the fuel level in the rear tank is higher than the front tank, it pumps from the rear tank into the front tank. It also somehow averages the sending units so the gauge on the panel shows the total fuel level or I guess the average fuel level of both tanks. It's kind of crazy, but it works. In the last video, I bench tested the module and believe it or not, it's working fine. But, [clears throat] the owner doesn't seem too excited about using it. He asked me repeatedly if I could just put a switch on the dash. He really wants a switch on the dash. Currently, the module is bypassed. There's just a jumper wire from the front tank sending unit to the gauge. To use the auxiliary tank, we need to connect the auxiliary sending unit to the gauge and at the same time connect the auxiliary pump relay to ground. Since we're disabling all the automatic controls, I'd also like to have a warning light on the dash. So, maybe the pump doesn't get left on for days at a time. Not that that would ever happen. There was already a switch with a warning light in the dash that, as far as I can tell, wasn't doing anything. So, I figured I could just add a double-throw relay to switch the sending units. That should have worked. Technically, it does work, but something's not right. >> [bell] >> So, the light comes on when the pump turns off. Isn't that backwards?
